title: From manual mornings to a self-running reporting platform
excerpt: How I replaced a team's manual reporting cycle with an automated data-analytics platform that ingests ~100 sources and runs ~500 jobs a day.
body: Every analytics team I've worked with starts its week the same way: downloading exports, reconciling spreadsheets, refreshing dashboards, and emailing the same reports to the same people. It's slow, fragile, and a waste of people who could be solving harder problems.

body.h: The shift: from reports to a product

body: Instead of producing reports by hand, we built a platform that produces them on its own. It ingests data from across the business — Excel files, APIs, operational systems, databases — consolidates it into a governed warehouse, and delivers decision-ready reports on a schedule to inboxes, Power BI, Excel, and PDF.
Today it orchestrates roughly 100 data sources and 500 pipeline runs a day, all scheduled, retried on failure, and observable from a single monitoring console.

Three things mattered more than the technology. First, treating reporting as a governed product, not a pile of scripts — one auditable source of truth. Second, monitoring: every run reports its own health, so problems surface before stakeholders notice. Third, a ruthless focus on the decision each report drives, not the data it contains.

Reporting that used to take a team's mornings now runs itself, and the analysts moved from assembling reports to acting on them. That's the real win — not the automation, but what people do with the time it frees.

title: Cutting 60 hours a week of data entry
excerpt: Replacing manual supplier-file transcription with an automation that turns spreadsheets into validated, Salesforce-ready promo fact sheets.
body: At CPG distributors, sales coordinators lose about a third of every week re-typing supplier Excel files into Salesforce. It's slow, error-prone, and it pulls expensive sales talent away from selling.

body.h: The gap between the spreadsheet and the system

body: The fix wasn't a new platform — it was closing the gap between the file and the CRM. Drop a supplier file in a shared folder, and the tool matches items against the stock master, validates the data, flags issues (missing SKUs, off-quarter dates, channel problems), and produces a clean, Salesforce-ready promo fact sheet for approval in minutes.

It was built on tools the team already used — Salesforce/Aforza, Excel, existing approval flows — so there was nothing new to onboard. And it kept a human in the loop: the coordinator reviews and approves before anything is published, with a full audit trail preserved.

For one customer it freed 60+ hours a week across five coordinators — roughly 3,000 hours a year — and redeployed about 1.5 full-time roles from data entry back to selling, with near-zero transcription errors. Half-day files became minutes.
